2026-10-07-4.script: Ever wonder why your soda can feels ready to pop when you are flying high above the clouds? Here is the thing, it is all about invisible air pressure pushing from both the inside and the outside. Down on the ground, thick air pushes hard against the metal aluminum walls to keep everything stable. But as you climb way up into the sky, the surrounding air gets much thinner and weaker. Suddenly, the trapped gas bubbles inside your drink start expanding like crazy because they have no resistance. The metal stretches, the top bulges outward, and honestly, it is just waiting for a tiny crack to burst open. That is why opening a warm soda after a flight always turns into a sticky surprise. Would you dare open a shaken can at thirty thousand feet, or would you just hand it back?

Instead, the trees slowly parted to reveal that exact same old stone marker sitting right in front of me again. That old trail wasn't on any map.

Some circled the North Pacific in a giant loop of current, and some may have drifted into the Arctic ice. So a lost box of bath toys helped map how the ocean moves. Found one on the beach? The Trinidad Moruga Scorpion measures around 1,200,000 Scoville units and features a distinct stinger-like tail.
The Carolina Reaper measures about 1,600,000 Scoville units and held the Guinness World Record for approximately ten years.
Pepper X measures approximately 2,700,000 Scoville units and is currently recognized by Guinness World Records as the hottest pepper in the world.

2026-10-10-3.idea_title: The Cave Found by 4 Teenagers in 1940
key_facts: In September 1940, four teenagers discovered the Lascaux cave near Montignac, France.
Marcel Ravidat initially found the hole, reportedly guided by his dog Robot.
He returned with three friends and a lamp to squeeze inside and explore.
The cave walls were adorned with hundreds of paintings of animals such as horses, bulls, and deer in red, yellow, and black pigments.
The paintings at Lascaux date back approximately 17,000 years.
Carbon dioxide, heat, and humidity from crowds of visitors began damaging the paintings.
Lascaux was permanently closed to the public in 1963 to preserve the artwork.
Modern visitors view exact replicas of the cave instead.

So in nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public. Today, visitors see exact replicas instead. Four teens, one lamp, and one of the greatest art discoveries ever. What would you paint for people seventeen thousand years from now? Tell me below. And what would you do if you found a hole in the ground…

2026-10-11-4.script: Before you carve your pumpkin, you should know why the first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips. Here's how Halloween's famous decoration swapped vegetables. Long ago in Ireland, people carved faces into big turnips and potatoes. Scotland used turnips too, and in England, large beets. They put a light inside and set them by windows and doors, to scare away wandering spirits. Picture a small, wrinkly turnip face glowing at you. Way creepier than a pumpkin. The name comes from an Irish folktale about a trickster called Stingy Jack. His ghostly light was Jack of the Lantern, later shortened to jack-o'-lantern. Then families from Ireland, Scotland and England moved to America. There they found pumpkins, which are native to the Americas. Bigger, hollow, and way easier to carve than a rock-hard turnip. So your jack-o'-lantern is a pumpkin because it was an upgrade. Would you dare carve a turnip this year? Either way, here's the one thing to remember this October.

2026-10-12-4.idea_title: The Eiffel Tower Had a 20-Year Expiry Date
key_facts: The Eiffel Tower opened for the World's Fair in 1889.
Gustave Eiffel's deal only let him use the land for 20 years before Paris could take it down.
Eiffel used scientific experiments, weather tests, and air resistance studies to justify keeping the tower.
In 1898, a Morse code radio message was sent from the tower across Paris.
Army radio tests from the top reached farther and farther, turning the tower into a giant antenna.
By 1909, a permanent radio station sat beneath the tower.
In 1910, Eiffel's deal was extended by 70 years because of its utility as a radio antenna.
2026-10-12-4.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the very first radio contact from the tower, in eighteen ninety-eight, reached the Pantheon about four kilometers away. What other landmark do you think has a secret second job?
2026-10-12-4.script: Before you visit Paris, you should know the Eiffel Tower had an expiry date. Here's how it almost came down, and what saved it. The tower opened for the World's Fair in eighteen eighty-nine. But Gustave Eiffel's deal only let him use the land for twenty years. After that, Paris could take it down. So Eiffel needed a reason to keep it. His answer? Science. He backed weather and air resistance experiments up there. Then in eighteen ninety-eight, a Morse code radio message was sent from the tower across Paris. Suddenly, the city's tallest structure looked like the perfect giant antenna. Army radio tests from the top reached farther and farther. By nineteen-oh-nine, a permanent radio station sat right beneath it. So in nineteen-ten, Eiffel's deal was extended by seventy years. That's how the tower beat its expiry date: it became an antenna. Did you know the Eiffel Tower almost came down, yes or no? If you said no, here's your reminder.

2026-10-13-3.script: Before you trust your map, you should know about Agloe, the town that was never supposed to exist. This is the true story of a fake town that became real. In the nineteen-twenties, two mapmakers wanted to catch copycats. So they invented a tiny town on a New York dirt road. They named it Agloe, from their initials. If Agloe showed up on another map, it was copied. Here's the twist. Around nineteen-thirty, a nearby fishing lodge took the name for real. The story goes that Agloe later turned up on a rival company's map. The rival said the name was now in real county records. The trap caught nothing, because the fake town had turned real. In twenty-fourteen, Agloe even landed in a US government database. So that's Agloe, the fake town people made real by believing the map. If you could invent one fake town, what would you name it? Tell me, and next time you open a map, think of Agloe.

2026-10-14-3.script: Why does a golf ball have dimples? You'd never guess the reason until you see the air. Here's how tiny dents make it fly farther. Fun part, early golfers noticed their beat-up, nicked balls flew farther than smooth new ones. So that's the reason, the dents help the air hold on, and a dimpled ball can fly about twice as far as a smooth one. How many dimples do you think are on a golf ball? 2026-10-14-4.script: You've squished it, but you've never known Play-Doh started out cleaning soot off walls in Cincinnati. Here's how a wall cleaner became a famous toy. In the nineteen-thirties, many homes burned coal, which left sooty grime on wallpaper. So a Cincinnati soap company called Kutol sold a doughy putty you'd roll over walls to lift the dirt. It was a wall cleaner for about twenty years. But after World War Two, families switched to oil and gas heat. Less soot, fewer dirty walls, and sales slid. Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall had her class make crafts with it. She told her brother-in-law, Joe McVicker, who ran the company, to sell it as a toy. In the mid nineteen-fifties, it got a new name, Play-Doh. So that's the twist, the toy in your hands was made to clean walls. What's the best thing you've made out of Play-Doh? So next time you squish it, think of a sooty wall in Cincinnati.

2026-10-15-1.idea_title: The Sleep Jump Up to 70% of People Get
key_facts: The sudden jolt before falling asleep is called a hypnic jerk.
Up to 70% of people experience hypnic jerks.
During sleep onset, muscles relax rapidly, which the brain may misread as falling.
The brain sends an emergency motor signal to contract muscles to catch the body.
Hypnic jerks are frequently accompanied by a sudden falling sensation.
An evolutionary hypothesis links hypnic jerks to tree-dwelling primate ancestors preventing falls.
Factors like stress, caffeine intake, and sleep deprivation increase the frequency of hypnic jerks.
Hypnic jerks are generally benign and harmless for most people.
2026-10-15-1.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some people get hypnic jerks almost every night, while most of us only get them now and then. Do you feel the jump, the falling, or both?

2026-10-15-1.script: Why does your body jump right before you fall asleep, and what is your brain actually doing? Here's what happens in that split second. That sudden jolt has a name, it's called a hypnic jerk. Sleep experts say up to seventy percent of people get them. As you drift off, your muscles relax, all at once. One idea is that your brain misreads all that relaxing as falling. So it fires your muscles to catch you. That's why it often comes with a quick falling feeling. Another idea goes back to our tree-sleeping ancestors, where a slip meant a real fall. Scientists say that one's still a guess, though. Stress, caffeine and too little sleep can make them happen more. And for most people, they're harmless. So that's what your brain is doing, it thinks you're falling, and it tries to catch you. Which do you get more, the jump or the falling feeling? Because tonight, right before you drift off, it might happen again.

Here are the five best fakers in nature. Number five, the death-feigning beetle.

It lies on its side looking dead, and when small fish come close, it strikes. Number two, the eastern hognose snake.
It rolls over, tongue out, and if you flip it upright, it rolls right back. Number one, the Virginia opossum.
It goes stiff, tongue out, and even gives off a stinky smell, sometimes for hours.
And it's not even trying, it happens automatically.
So the snake never quits when flipped, but the possum wins, it even smells the part. Which of these would fool you best?
Next time an animal lies perfectly still, ask yourself.

key_facts: The ring finger cannot easily lift independently when the middle finger is bent due to connecting fibrous tendon bands (juncturae tendinum).
Circling the right foot clockwise while drawing a number six with the right hand often causes the foot to involuntarily reverse direction due to ipsilateral motor coordination in the brain.
Between 65% and 81% of people can roll their tongue into a U shape.
Tongue rolling is not governed by a single dominant gene, as evidenced by identical twins who do not always share the trait.

Scientists aren't sure why, but one idea is your brain links plans for limbs on the same side. Trick three. Roll your tongue into a U. Roughly sixty-five to eighty-one percent of people can. Textbooks called it a simple gene, but identical twins don't always match. So now you know why your finger sticks, your foot flips, and your tongue might not roll. Which trick beat you? 2026-10-16-4.idea_title: Wobbly Table? 3 Fixes (One Is Pure Math)
key_facts: Wobbling is frequently caused by uneven floor contours rather than flawed table legs.
Many commercial and home tables feature built-in adjustable threaded screw feet.
Mathematical topology proofs demonstrate that rotating a square four-legged table on a continuously uneven floor guarantees a state where all four legs touch simultaneously.
A stable contact orientation occurs within a 90-degree (quarter turn) rotation.
Abrupt discontinuities like sharp tile thresholds or steps violate the theorem's continuity premise.
A rotation-stabilized table may rest at a slight incline, but rocking motion is eliminated.

Mathematicians proved that on a smooth, gently uneven floor, a square table with equal legs finds a spot where all four touch. Usually within a quarter turn, because the hovering leg has to touch down somewhere. It won't be perfectly level, and tile edges break it, but the rocking stops. 2026-10-17-3.idea_title: What Color Is the Sun? 3-Second Quiz
key_facts: The sun emits light across all visible wavelengths, making its actual color pure white.
Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light, causing the sun to appear yellow, orange, or red.
Polar bears have completely black skin underneath their fur to absorb and retain heat.
Polar bear cubs are born with pink skin that gradually turns black within several months.
Individual strands of polar bear fur are hollow and translucent, appearing white only due to light scattering.
Baby flamingos hatch with grey or dull white down feathers.
Flamingos develop their distinctive pink color by absorbing carotenoid pigments found in their diet of brine shrimp and algae.

2026-10-17-3.script: Before you scroll, what color is the sun? Hint, it's not yellow. Three color questions, three seconds each. Lock in your answer. Question one. What color is the sun, really? Three, two, one. White! Sunlight is almost pure white. Our air makes it look yellow, especially when it's low in the sky. Question two. What color is a polar bear's skin? Three, two, one. Black! 2026-10-17-4.idea_title: How Popcorn Pops: 135 PSI Inside One Kernel
key_facts: Before popping, pressure inside a popcorn kernel reaches about 9 times atmospheric pressure (135 PSI).
Each kernel contains a small droplet of water surrounded by hard starch inside a tough outer shell called the hull.
Heating turns the trapped water into superheated steam that cannot escape the waterproof hull.
The kernel heats up to approximately 347 degrees Fahrenheit (175 degrees Celsius).
The intense heat turns the internal starch into a gelatinous, molten gel.
At approximately 135 PSI, the hull ruptures violently.
As the pressure drops instantly, the superheated gel inflates into airy foam that solidifies into a fluffy shape up to 50 times its original size.
Popcorn jumps because the initial burst of expanding starch pushes forcefully against the pan like a leg kicking off the ground.

2026-10-18-1.idea_title: Why New Baseballs Get 30 Seconds of Mud
key_facts: Every Major League baseball is rubbed with mud before game use to remove slickness.
Brand new factory baseballs have a glossy, slippery sheen that makes them hard for pitchers to grip.
Early teams experimented with tobacco juice, shoe polish, and bleacher dirt to dull the shine.
In 1938, coach Lena Blackburne discovered a unique silt mud along a New Jersey riverbank that perfected the process.
The mud is uniquely fine and described as feeling like chocolate pudding and cold cream.
The exact geographic location where the mud is harvested remains a closely guarded secret.
Each MLB club receives roughly 10 pounds of the mud per season.
Each individual game ball is rubbed for at least 30 seconds before use.

Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland consists of approximately 40,000 predominantly hexagonal basalt columns formed by cooling volcanic lava.
Zhangye Danxia in China gets its rainbow-striped mountains from layered mineral deposits like iron oxide laid down over millions of years.
Lake Hillier in Australia maintains a permanent bubble-gum pink color caused primarily by salt-loving microalgae, remaining pink even when placed in a glass.
Caño Cristales in Colombia becomes the 'river of five colors' when the endemic aquatic plant Macarenia clavigera blooms bright red under specific light and water conditions.
Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat on Earth.
Seasonal rainwater over Salar de Uyuni forms an expansive, ultra-thin sheet of water that creates the world's largest natural mirror.

key_facts: Movie theaters use Flavacol, a fine salt containing artificial butter flavor and yellow food dyes, to season popcorn.

Commercial poppers use high pressure and heat to coat every kernel evenly while popping.

2026-10-19-3.idea_title: The Space Signal Heard Once in 1977
key_facts: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope in Ohio detected a strong narrowband radio signal.
Big Ear was a fixed telescope that used Earth's rotation to sweep across the sky.
The signal originated from the constellation Sagittarius and lasted for 72 seconds, matching the telescope's window of observation for a celestial point source.
The alphanumeric sequence 6EQUJ5 represented signal intensity, where letters corresponded to values exceeding 9.
Astronomer Jerry Ehman discovered the signal on computer printouts, circled it in red pen, and wrote 'Wow!'.
Subsequent searches by multiple radio telescopes failed to detect a repeat signal.
In 2024, researchers proposed that a rare magnetar flare exciting an interstellar hydrogen cloud could potentially explain the emission.

The printout showed a strange code: six, E, Q, U, J, five. Letters meant extra strong. An astronomer circled it in red ink and wrote: Wow. Telescopes went back again and again. Nothing. In twenty twenty-four, scientists suggested a magnetar flare may have made a hydrogen cloud flash. It's still just an idea. So that's the Wow signal: seventy-two seconds, one word, no repeat. 2026-10-20-1.idea_title: How Desert Ice Houses Worked 2,400 Years Ago
key_facts: Ancient Persians engineered ice houses known as yakhchals over 2,400 years ago without electricity.
Water was channeled from underground aqueducts (qanats) into long, shallow outdoor basins.
A massive, tall adobe wall shielded the shallow pools from solar radiation throughout the day.
Through radiative cooling, the water shed heat directly into the clear, dry night sky and froze during winter nights.
Ice blocks were harvested and moved into an enormous, thick-walled mudbrick cone.
Thermal convection allowed warm air to escape through a top apex vent while cold, dense air sank into a deep subterranean pit.
Layered with insulating straw, stored ice remained frozen through extreme desert summer heat.

key_facts: Roman builders hot-mixed quicklime with volcanic ash and water.
The intense heat of hot-mixing left small, brittle white lime clasts inside the concrete.
Historically, researchers assumed these lime clasts were the result of poor or sloppy mixing.
When cracks propagate through Roman concrete, they naturally travel directly through the weaker lime clasts.
Infiltrating rainwater dissolves calcium from the exposed lime clasts, forming a calcium-saturated solution.
The calcium solution recrystallizes into solid calcium carbonate (limestone), sealing the crack.
Laboratory tests demonstrated these cracks self-healed within approximately two weeks.

2026-10-21-4.idea_title: The Bank Built From the Mail in 1916
key_facts: The Bank of Vernal in Vernal, Utah was built in 1916.
Bricks were shipped through the parcel post mail service because freight costs were too high.
The bricks traveled 427 miles via trains, wagons, and ferryboats.
Estimates of the number of bricks range from 15,000 to 80,000.
The massive volume of mailed bricks caused the postmaster to complain, leading to a new rule capping shipments at 200 pounds a day per sender.
The brick bank building is still standing today.

2026-10-21-4.script: How would you get a bank built when shipping bricks cost a fortune? This town mailed them. This is the true story of a bank that came by mail. It's nineteen-sixteen in Vernal, Utah, a town with no railroad of its own. A businessman wants a fancy brick front, but the bricks are hundreds of miles away. Freight costs a fortune. The new parcel post service costs about half. So the bricks get packed into small packages and mailed. They ride trains, wagons and ferryboats, four hundred and twenty-seven miles. Most reports say eighty thousand bricks. A postal historian says about fifteen thousand. Either way, the post office is buried in bricks, and the postmaster complains to Washington. Soon, a new rule: two hundred pounds a day, max, from one sender to one person. Too late. The bank goes up, and it's still standing today. What's the weirdest thing you've ever gotten in the mail? So if you ever need a building delivered, ask yourself...

2026-10-22-1.idea_title: How A Click Pen Works in 2 Clicks
key_facts: A retractable click pen operates using a plunger, a crown-shaped rotating cam, and a spring.
The plunger has straight teeth that mesh with slanted teeth on the cam.
The angled teeth force the cam to rotate a step each time the plunger presses down.
Releasing the plunger allows the spring to push the cam onto an internal barrel ledge, locking the pen tip out.
A second click forces the cam off the ledge and twists it into alignment with vertical channels.
The spring pulls the ink cartridge and tip back inside the barrel when aligned with the channels.
A full extend-and-retract cycle takes two clicks and two cam rotations.

2026-10-22-1.script: You've clicked a pen thousands of times, but you've never seen what spins inside it. Your thumb pushes a plunger with tiny teeth. They press a little crown with slanted teeth, called a cam. The slants twist it one step. Let go, and the spring lifts it onto a ledge. Tip locked out. Click again, and it slips off the ledge and twists once more. Now it misses the ledge, and the spring pulls the tip in. Two twists, one spring, every single click.

2026-10-22-2.idea_title: 30 Cats vs a Square Made of Nothing 😂
key_facts: In 2021, researchers published a citizen science experiment testing domestic cats with the Kanizsa square visual illusion.
The illusion uses four circular shapes with wedges removed resembling Pac-Man, arranged so human and animal brains perceive a phantom square contour.
Cat owners were instructed to wear sunglasses indoors during trials to avoid involuntary eye-gaze cueing.
Hundreds of owners enrolled, but only 30 cats completed all daily testing protocols.
Cats chose to sit inside the illusory Kanizsa square just as frequently as inside an actual taped square outline.

Taped to the floor, their mouths line up, so your brain sees a square that isn't there. Owners also taped down a real square, and the same Pac-Men facing the wrong way. And so they wouldn't give the cats hints, the owners wore sunglasses. Indoors. For science. Hundreds signed up, but only thirty cats finished, because, well, cats. So, did the cats fall for it? Yes. They sat inside the fake square about as often as the real one. So "if I fits, I sits" works even when there's nothing to fit in. Would your cat sit in the paper square, or ignore it completely? 2026-10-23-1.idea_title: How Archimedes' Screw Works (2,200 Years Old)
key_facts: An Archimedes screw lifts liquid uphill without a pressurized motor.
It consists of a helical spiral enclosed tightly within a cylinder placed at an incline.
Rotating the screw scoops a isolated pocket of water at the base.
Gravity keeps the water at the lowest point of each turn, which physically shifts upward as the screw rotates.
If the angle of tilt is too steep, the water slips over the blades and fails to rise.
Modern wastewater treatment and drainage plants still utilize large Archimedes screws today.
2026-10-23-1.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some modern Archimedes screws run in reverse, letting water fall down them to spin a generator. If you had to lift water without a motor, how would you do it?

Scientists wondered what caused the movement since the 1940s.
Researchers fitted fifteen rocks with GPS trackers and cameras.

Thin ice and wind were proven to be the cause of the moving rocks.

2026-10-23-4.script: You'd think rocks can't move by themselves. In Death Valley, they left tracks hundreds of feet long. Here's the true story of how scientists finally caught them moving. On a dry, flat lakebed called Racetrack Playa, rocks sit at the end of long, wandering trails. Nobody had ever seen one move. Since the nineteen-forties, scientists wondered what pushed them. Wind? Mud? Something stranger? So a team of researchers fitted fifteen rocks with GPS trackers and set up cameras. They thought they might be waiting for years. In December twenty-thirteen, rain made a shallow pond there, and it froze overnight. In the sun, the ice cracked into huge panels thinner than a phone. A light breeze pushed the panels, and they shoved the rocks along a few inches per second. So the rocks never moved themselves. Thin ice and a light wind did the pushing. key_facts: The end hook on a tape measure is intentionally loose and wobbly, not broken.
Pulling the blade winds an internal flat coiled spring around the center hub.
Releasing the blade allows the tensioned coiled spring to unwind and retract the blade automatically.
The blade is manufactured with a curved, concave cross-section that gives it structural rigidity across long spans without collapsing.
The rivets holding the hook sit in elongated slots allowing it to slide back and forth.
When hooked over an outside edge, the hook slides out by exactly its own thickness to measure from the inside face.
When pushed against an inside surface, the hook slides in by its own thickness to measure from the outside face.
This sliding mechanism ensures that both inside and outside measurements start at true zero.

2026-10-25-101.idea_title: Why do leaves turn orange in fall?
key_facts: Yellow/orange carotenoids are in leaves all year, masked by more abundant green chlorophyll (USDA Forest Service)
In fall, shorter days and cooler temps make trees stop replacing chlorophyll, so the green fades (USDA Forest Service)
Red pigments are newly formed in fall from sugars trapped in the leaf (USDA Forest Service)
A layer of cork cells forms at the base of the leaf stalk and the leaf falls (USDA Forest Service)
Trees pull back roughly half or more of the leaf's nitrogen before it drops; a fallen leaf keeps ~40% of its summer nitrogen (EarthWise)

2026-10-25-101.script:
Why do leaves turn orange in fall?
Here's the twist:
the orange was there all summer.
A leaf is packed with green chlorophyll,
the pigment that turns sunlight into sugar.
But it's also holding yellow and orange pigments,
called carotenoids.
All summer, the green drowns them out.
Then the nights get longer,
and the tree shuts the leaf down.
It stops making chlorophyll,
and breaks the old green apart.
Scientists think it pulls back about half the leaf's nitrogen,
saving it for spring.
With the green gone,
the hidden orange shows through.
And the reds?
Those are brand new.
Trapped sugars turn into red pigments,
right before a cork-like seal forms at the stem,
and the leaf lets go.
So fall doesn't paint the leaves.
It peels the green away.
Which tree turns the brightest where you live?

key_facts: Hypocaust = 'heat from below': floor raised on pilae so furnace (praefurnium) gases flow underneath (Wikipedia: Hypocaust, Praefurnium)
Vitruvius credits Sergius Orata (fl. c. 95 BC), an oyster farmer who popularised 'hanging baths'; attribution not fully established (Wikipedia: Sergius Orata)

2026-10-25-102.script:
How did the Romans heat their floors,
without a single wire?
Two thousand years ago,
in the middle of winter,
a Roman could walk across a stone floor barefoot,
and it would be warm.
The trick was hiding under their feet.
It's called a hypocaust,
which means "heat from below."
The Roman writer Vitruvius
credits a businessman named Sergius Orata,
around 95 BC.
Orata got rich farming oysters,
and he sold wealthy Romans on heated "hanging baths."
Soon, no fancy villa was complete without one.
So how did it work?
Start with a furnace,
called the praefurnium,
built just outside the room, a little lower down.
Slaves fed it wood all day.
Now, instead of laying the floor on the ground,
the Romans lifted it up.
They built short stacks of square bricks,
called pilae,
row after row.
Vitruvius says two feet tall.
On top went big two-foot tiles,
then a thick layer of concrete,
then the floor you'd walk on.
That left a hollow space underneath,
like a crawl space made for smoke.
The fire's hot air and smoke
rushed into that gap,
swirled between the pillars,
and soaked heat into the floor above.
But it didn't stop there.
Hollow clay pipes, called tubuli,
ran up inside the walls.
Hot air climbed through them,
warming the walls too,
then escaped through vents near the roof.
So the whole room became a radiator.
Here's a detail Vitruvius was oddly specific about.
The floor underneath should slope toward the furnace,
so if you threw a ball in,
it couldn't stop inside.
It would roll right back to the fire.
Romans also lined up their rooms by heat.
The caldarium, the hot room,
sat closest to the furnace.
Next came the warm room,
the tepidarium.
And the cold plunge pool, the frigidarium,
sat farthest away.
So, how hot did it get?
In modern tests on rebuilt Roman baths,
the floors reached twenty to fifty degrees Celsius.
Hot enough that bathers wore wooden-soled sandals.
The hot room's air sat around thirty-two degrees,
thick with steam.
And all of it ran on wood.
The giant Baths of Caracalla in Rome
reportedly burned around ten tons of wood,
every single day.
When the empire fell apart,
so did the skills and the labor
that kept these furnaces burning.
For centuries,
much of Europe went back to smoky open fires.
But the idea never died.
In Korea, the ondol system
runs fire smoke under the floor in a very similar way.
And today's underfloor heating
does exactly what the Romans did:
warm the floor,
and let the heat rise.
Just with pipes instead of pillars,
and nobody shoveling wood.
Would you trade your radiator
for a Roman floor?

key_facts: Alpacas hum with their mouths closed when they are uneasy or nervous.
Giraffes produce a low nocturnal humming vocalization that resembles eerie low-frequency sound.

Male koalas produce deep bellows about 20 times lower in pitch than expected for their body size, using unique extra vocal folds.
The Australian superb lyrebird is renowned for mimicking artificial sounds, including car alarms, camera shutters, and chainsaws.

key_facts: In 1968, 3M scientist Spencer Silver invented a low-tack, reusable adhesive while trying to create a super strong glue.
The adhesive remained unused at 3M for five years.
In 1974, coworker Art Fry used the adhesive to keep bookmarks from falling out of his choir songbook.
After initial commercial failure in 1977, free sample distributions in Boise, Idaho in 1978 won consumers over.
Post-it notes officially launched across the United States in 1980.
The iconic yellow color was selected purely by chance because the adjacent laboratory only had yellow scrap paper available.

For five years, nobody at the company knew what it was for. Then in nineteen seventy-four, a coworker's bookmarks kept falling out of his choir songbook. He tried the weak glue, and the bookmark stayed put, then peeled off clean. After a flop in nineteen seventy-seven, free samples in Boise, Idaho won people over. They went on sale across America in nineteen eighty, yellow because that was the scrap paper next door. So the glue waited five years because it was a solution without a problem, until a bookmark. key_facts: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation
A vacuum flask is two walls with a vacuum between them, which blocks conduction and convection
Silvered/shiny walls reflect infrared radiation back
Invented by Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892 to store liquefied gases
Most remaining heat loss is through the stopper/lid
Good flasks keep drinks hot for around 12 hours

2026-10-26-101.script:
How does a thermos keep coffee hot
for twelve whole hours?
Heat escapes in three ways.
It can touch its way out,
that's conduction.
It can ride on moving air,
that's convection.
Or it can glow away as invisible light,
called radiation.
A thermos blocks all three.
It's really two bottles,
one inside the other,
and the gap between them is a vacuum.
With no air in there,
heat has nothing to touch,
and nothing to ride.
Then the walls are shiny,
like a mirror,
so the glow bounces back into your coffee.
A scientist named James Dewar
invented it in 1892,
to keep liquid gases ice cold.
The only real leak?
The lid.
So what's the longest your coffee ever stayed hot?

2026-10-26-102.idea_title: How does a plane toilet flush at 35,000 feet?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing

2026-10-26-102.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?

2026-10-26-103.idea_title: What happens to your food after you swallow it? (the digestive journey)
key_facts: Ancient physicians described digestion as 'concoction', a kind of cooking in the stomach; in the 1750s Réaumur fed a bird food in perforated metal tubes and the food still dissolved (Popular Science Monthly, 1909)
Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)
2026-10-26-103.pinned_comment: Which food do you think takes the longest trip through your body? 🍙
2026-10-26-103.script:
What actually happens to your food,
after you swallow it?
It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?

00:02:46,310 --> 00:02:48,210

00:02:48,510 --> 00:02:49,780
slip into your blood.

74
00:02:50,330 --> 00:02:52,850
What's left moves on to the large intestine.

75
00:02:53,400 --> 00:02:56,570

00:03:07,780 --> 00:03:09,880

2026-10-26-104.idea_title: How did people in old Japan smell what time it was? (incense clocks)
key_facts: Seal-type incense clocks (Japanese ko-dokei) laid a continuous trail of incense powder in a pattern pressed into flattened ash with a stamp or stencil
The powder burned at a fairly steady rate, so elapsed time could be read from how far the ember had travelled
Markers or tablets of different incense placed along the trail changed the aroma when reached, so an attendant could tell the time by smell
Burn times ranged from about 12 hours to a month, depending on trail length
Some versions dropped balls into a tray when the incense burned through, as an audible signal
Incense clocks came to Japan from China and were used in Japan from the Nara period

2026-10-26-104.script:
How did people in old Japan
smell what time it was?
No gears. No ticking.
Just a box of ash.
First, they smoothed white ash flat,
and pressed a stamp into it.
That left a groove,
a maze that snakes back and forth.
They filled the groove with incense powder:
one long, thin trail.
Light one end,
and a tiny ember crawls through the maze,
at a nearly steady speed.
Here's the clever part.
At set marks along the trail,
they switched to a different incense.
So when the smell in the room changed,
you knew more time had passed.
Some trails burned for twelve hours.
Some lasted a whole month.
A few even dropped a little ball
onto a tray, like an alarm.
So, what time does your room smell like right now?

2026-10-26-106.idea_title: How does a plane toilet flush at 35,000 feet?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing
2026-10-26-106.pinned_comment: Have you ever jumped when a plane toilet flushed? Be honest 😂
2026-10-26-106.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?

2026-10-26-107.idea_title: What happens to your food after you swallow it? (the digestive journey)
key_facts: Ancient physicians described digestion as 'concoction', a kind of cooking in the stomach; in the 1750s Réaumur fed a bird food in perforated metal tubes and the food still dissolved (Popular Science Monthly, 1909)
Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)
2026-10-26-107.pinned_comment: Which food do you think takes the longest trip through your body? 🍙
2026-10-26-107.script:
What actually happens to your food,
after you swallow it?
It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?

00:00:24,590 --> 00:00:25,890
but it still dissolved.

13
00:00:26,440 --> 00:00:29,100
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani

14
00:00:29,400 --> 00:00:31,010
even tried it on himself,

15
00:00:31,310 --> 00:00:33,560
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.

16
00:00:34,110 --> 00:00:35,620
The answer was a liquid.

17
00:00:36,170 --> 00:00:37,840
He called it gastric juice.

18
00:00:38,390 --> 00:00:39,880
So let's follow one bite,

19
00:00:40,180 --> 00:00:41,260
all the way through.

20
00:00:41,810 --> 00:00:43,120
Step one: your mouth.

21
00:00:43,670 --> 00:00:45,570
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,

22
00:00:45,870 --> 00:00:47,120
and saliva soaks it.

23
00:00:47,670 --> 00:00:50,190
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,

24
00:00:50,490 --> 00:00:52,520
that starts turning starch into sugar,

25
00:00:52,820 --> 00:00:54,190
before you even swallow.

26
00:00:54,740 --> 00:00:56,710
Then your tongue pushes the food back,

27
00:00:57,010 --> 00:00:59,030
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,

28
00:00:59,330 --> 00:01:01,220
folds down over your windpipe,

29
00:01:01,520 --> 00:01:03,270
so nothing goes the wrong way.

30
00:01:03,820 --> 00:01:05,930
Now the food enters the esophagus,

31
00:01:06,230 --> 00:01:09,190
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.

32
00:01:09,740 --> 00:01:10,950
It doesn't just fall.

33
00:01:11,500 --> 00:01:13,480
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,

34
00:01:13,780 --> 00:01:15,360
like toothpaste in a tube.

35
00:01:15,910 --> 00:01:17,420
That's called peristalsis.

36
00:01:17,970 --> 00:01:19,940
The trip takes about nine seconds,

37
00:01:20,240 --> 00:01:22,050
and it works even upside down.

38
00:01:22,600 --> 00:01:23,920
Next stop, the stomach.

39
00:01:24,470 --> 00:01:26,110
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,

40
00:01:26,410 --> 00:01:28,230
filled with hydrochloric acid.

41
00:01:28,780 --> 00:01:31,430
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,

42
00:01:31,730 --> 00:01:33,620
about as sour as lemon juice.

43
00:01:34,170 --> 00:01:35,820
It kills a lot of germs,

44
00:01:36,120 --> 00:01:38,000
and helps an enzyme called pepsin

45
00:01:38,300 --> 00:01:39,840
start chopping up protein.

46
00:01:40,390 --> 00:01:41,890
About three times a minute,

47
00:01:42,190 --> 00:01:44,190
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,

48
00:01:44,490 --> 00:01:47,180
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.

49
00:01:47,730 --> 00:01:49,620
That can take two to four hours.

50
00:01:50,170 --> 00:01:52,650
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?

51
00:01:53,200 --> 00:01:55,460
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,

52
00:01:55,760 --> 00:01:57,970
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.

53
00:01:58,520 --> 00:02:01,560
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.

54
00:02:02,110 --> 00:02:03,710
Then a little valve opens,

55
00:02:04,010 --> 00:02:06,500
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,

56
00:02:06,800 --> 00:02:08,320
into the small intestine.

57
00:02:08,870 --> 00:02:11,160
This is where the real magic happens.

58
00:02:11,710 --> 00:02:13,330
It's about five meters long,

59
00:02:13,630 --> 00:02:15,260
coiled up inside your belly.

60
00:02:15,810 --> 00:02:17,240
Your liver sends in bile,

61
00:02:17,540 --> 00:02:19,800
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.

62
00:02:20,350 --> 00:02:22,340
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,

63
00:02:22,640 --> 00:02:24,340
and neutralizes the acid.

64
00:02:24,890 --> 00:02:28,110
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,

65
00:02:28,410 --> 00:02:29,320
called villi,

66
00:02:29,620 --> 00:02:32,770
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.

67
00:02:33,320 --> 00:02:36,300
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining

68
00:02:36,600 --> 00:02:38,850
covers about thirty-two square meters.

69
00:02:39,400 --> 00:02:41,050
That's half a badminton court!

70
00:02:41,600 --> 00:02:43,690
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,

71
00:02:43,990 --> 00:02:45,760
but half a court is still huge.

72
00:02:46,310 --> 00:02:48,210
Right here, most of the nutrients

73
00:02:48,510 --> 00:02:49,780
slip into your blood.

74
00:02:50,330 --> 00:02:52,850
What's left moves on to the large intestine.

75
00:02:53,400 --> 00:02:56,570
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.

76
00:02:57,120 --> 00:02:59,180
Its main job is soaking up water.

77
00:02:59,730 --> 00:03:01,950
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.

78
00:03:02,500 --> 00:03:05,700
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,

79
00:03:06,000 --> 00:03:07,230
mostly right here.

80
00:03:07,780 --> 00:03:09,880
They munch the fiber you can't digest,

81
00:03:10,180 --> 00:03:12,050
and make some vitamins in return.

82
00:03:12,600 --> 00:03:14,620
So how long does the whole trip take?

83
00:03:15,170 --> 00:03:18,200
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,

84
00:03:18,500 --> 00:03:21,550
and up to another two days in the large intestine.

85
00:03:22,100 --> 00:03:23,890
Whatever your body can't use,

86
00:03:24,190 --> 00:03:25,250
leaves at the end.

87
00:03:25,800 --> 00:03:26,660
But the rest?

88
00:03:27,210 --> 00:03:28,950
That bite became your energy,

89
00:03:29,250 --> 00:03:30,140
your muscles,

90
00:03:30,440 --> 00:03:32,510
even the thoughts you're having right now.

91
00:03:33,060 --> 00:03:34,430
So which food do you think

92
00:03:34,730 --> 00:03:36,100
takes the longest trip?

2026-10-26-107.title: What Happens to Food in the 2 Days After You Swallow It

2026-10-26-108.idea_title: Why do bats sleep upside down?
key_facts: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight
Bat wings can't generate enough lift from a standstill on the ground, and their hind legs are too small and light to run for a takeoff
Hanging lets them simply let go and drop into flight
Tendons in the feet are pulled tight by the bat's body weight, closing the claws with no muscle effort; muscles are needed to open them
Bats are light enough that blood pooling in the head is not a problem
Roosting high keeps them out of reach of most predators
Some species like the little brown bat sleep around 19-20 hours a day
2026-10-26-108.pinned_comment: Could you nap upside down like a bat? How long do you think you'd last? 🦇
2026-10-26-108.script:
You'd pass out sleeping upside down,
but some bats do it 20 hours a day.
So why hang like that?
Bats have a takeoff problem.
They're the only mammals that truly fly,
but their wings can't lift them off the ground,
and their back legs are too tiny to run.
So they sleep up high, hanging by their toes.
Time to go?
They let go, drop,
and they're flying before they hit anything.
But doesn't hanging all day get tiring?
Nope.
Their toe tendons work like a locking clip.
Body weight pulls the tendon tight,
and the claws clamp shut, with zero effort.
To let go, they use muscles to open them.
And the blood rush to the head?
Bats are so light, it barely happens.
Plus, up high, most predators can't reach them.
So, could you nap upside down like a bat?

2026-10-27-101.idea_title: How do smoke detectors know there's a fire?
key_facts: Ionization smoke alarms contain a small amount of americium-241, which emits alpha particles
Alpha particles ionize air between two electrodes, sustaining a small steady current
Smoke entering the chamber disrupts/reduces the current; below a threshold the alarm sounds
Photoelectric alarms shine an LED across a chamber away from a photocell; smoke scatters light onto the sensor
Americium-241 half-life is about 432 years (EPA: 432.2)
Smoke alarms are typically replaced about every 10 years
2026-10-27-101.pinned_comment: Check the label on yours: does it say ionization (radioactive) or photoelectric (light)? Tell me which one you've got 👇
2026-10-27-101.script:
Your smoke alarm might be radioactive.
Nobody tells you,
but that's how it smells smoke.
Inside sits a speck of americium,
which fires out tiny alpha particles.
They slam into the air
between two metal plates,
knocking electrons loose.
Now the air carries electricity,
so a tiny, steady current flows.
When smoke drifts in,
bits of smoke grab those charged particles.
The current drops,
and the alarm screams.
Other alarms use light instead.
An LED shines across a dark chamber,
away from a sensor.
No smoke, no light hits it.
But smoke scatters the beam,
bouncing light into the sensor.
Beep!
And that americium?
Its half-life is four hundred thirty-two years,
so it outlasts your alarm by centuries.
So, is the one above your bed
radioactive, or running on light?
